description: The sit-up is a full range spinal flexion exercise that targets the rectus abdominis and hip flexors. It provides a greater range of motion than the crunch.
tips: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Place your hands behind your head or crossed over your chest. Curl your entire upper body off the floor, reaching toward your knees. Lower back down with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: Hip abduction exercises target the gluteus medius and minimus, which are crucial for hip stability, knee alignment, and single-leg athletic movements. Commonly performed on a machine or with a band.
tips: Sit on the hip abduction machine with pads on the outside of your thighs. Press your legs apart against the resistance by contracting your outer glutes. Hold briefly at the end range. Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

nameEs: Abducción de cadera en decúbito lateral
description: Side-lying hip abduction is a direct glute medius strengthening exercise requiring no equipment. It trains the hip in the frontal plane, which is neglected by most squat and lunge patterns. Critical for knee stability and hip alignment.
tips: Lie on your side with body in a straight line, bottom knee slightly bent for support. Keep the top leg straight with foot flexed. Lift the top leg to approximately 45°, keeping toes pointing forward. Hold 1 second at the top. Lower slowly. Perform 3x15-20 per side.
commonMistakes: Keep the top leg straight throughout. Foot flexed, toes pointing forward — not up. Do not let the hip roll backward. Add an ankle weight for progression.

description: Hip adduction exercises target the adductor muscles of the inner thigh. Commonly performed on a machine or with cable, it strengthens hip stability and groin muscles.
tips: Sit on the hip adduction machine and adjust the pads to the outside of your thighs. Select the desired weight. Bring your thighs together against the resistance by contracting your inner thighs. Hold briefly at the end. Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The clamshell is the foundational glute medius exercise. Performed lying on your side with knees bent, it isolates the glute medius and external hip rotators — the muscles that prevent knee valgus (collapse) in squats and lunges. Essential for beginners and as a warm-up for all lower body training.
tips: Lie on your side with hips and knees bent at 45°. Stack your legs. Keeping feet together, rotate your top knee upward like a clamshell opening. Keep the pelvis still. Hold at the top for 1 second. Lower slowly. Perform 3x15-20 per side.
commonMistakes: Keep the pelvis completely still — do not rotate the hip back to lift higher. The range of motion is intentionally small. Add a resistance band above the knees for progression.

description: The band pull-apart is a foundational rear delt and upper back exercise that requires only a resistance band. It directly counteracts the forward shoulder posture caused by excessive pushing movements, making it essential for any home or calisthenics training program.
tips: Hold a resistance band with both hands at shoulder height, arms extended in front of you. With straight arms, pull the band apart by moving both hands outward to your sides. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end range. Slowly return to start. Perform 3x15-20 reps.
commonMistakes: Keep arms straight throughout. Squeeze shoulder blades together at the end of each rep. Start with a light band and focus on form.

description: The chest opener stretch counters the rounded posture from pressing exercises and desk work by stretching the pectorals, anterior deltoids, and biceps through shoulder retraction and extension.
tips: Stand or sit tall. Clasp your hands behind your back with arms extended. Gently squeeze your shoulder blades together and lift your hands away from your body while opening your chest toward the ceiling. Hold 20-30 seconds. Release and repeat.

description: The dumbbell fly is an isolation exercise for the pectoralis major. The wide arc motion stretches the chest at the bottom for an enhanced mind-muscle connection and growth stimulus.
tips: Lie on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand, arms extended above chest. Lower the dumbbells out and down in a wide arc, keeping a slight bend in the elbows. Stop when you feel a deep chest stretch. Bring the dumbbells back together in the same arc. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The dumbbell chest fly is an isolation exercise for the pectoralis major. The wide arcing motion stretches the chest more than pressing movements, promoting muscle length development.
tips: Lie on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with arms extended above your chest, palms facing each other. With a slight bend in the elbows, lower the dumbbells out to your sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch in your chest. Bring the dumbbells back together above your chest in the same arc. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The cable chest fly uses pulleys set at mid-height to provide constant tension throughout the fly motion, making it superior to dumbbell flys for continuous chest loading.
tips: Set dual cable pulleys to chest height. Stand in the middle and grip each handle with one hand, stepping forward slightly. With a slight bend in the elbows, bring both handles forward and together in a hugging motion. Squeeze your chest at the top. Slowly open your arms back to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The bird dog is a core stability exercise that trains anti-rotation and spinal stabilization by extending opposite limbs from a quadruped position. It is key for lower back health.
tips: Start on hands and knees with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Engage your core. Extend your right arm and left leg simultaneously until both are parallel to the floor. Hold for 2-3 seconds. Return to starting position. Switch to left arm and right leg. Continue alternating for desired reps.

description: The good morning is a hinge movement that strengthens the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back erectors under load. Performed with a barbell on the upper back, it is a key accessory for deadlift and squat strength.
tips: Place a barbell on your upper back as in a squat. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent. Hinge forward at the hips, pushing them back while keeping your back flat and chest up. Lower your torso until it is nearly parallel to the floor. Drive your hips forward to return to standing. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The burpee is a full-body functional exercise combining a squat, push-up, and jump. It develops cardiovascular fitness, strength, and coordination simultaneously with no equipment required.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Squat down and place hands on the floor in front of you. Jump or step feet back into a plank position. Perform a push-up. Jump feet back toward your hands into a squat. Explosively jump up with arms overhead. Land softly and immediately go into the next rep.

description: The farmer's walk is a loaded carry exercise that develops total body strength, grip endurance, traps, and core stability. It is highly functional and transfers to everyday activities.
tips: Pick up a heavy dumbbell, kettlebell, or trap bar in each hand. Stand tall with shoulders retracted and core braced. Walk forward for the desired distance taking short controlled steps. Keep the weights at your sides without letting them touch your body. Maintain upright posture throughout.

description: Incline walking on a treadmill increases cardiovascular demand and glute/hamstring activation compared to flat walking, making it an effective low-impact fat-burning exercise.
tips: Set the treadmill to an incline between 5-15 percent. Walk at a moderate pace (3-4 mph) without holding the handrails. Maintain upright posture and take natural strides. Breathe steadily throughout. Adjust incline and speed to match your fitness level and goals.

description: Cycling is a low-impact cardiovascular exercise that strengthens the legs and improves aerobic capacity. It can be performed outdoors or on a stationary bike.
tips: Adjust the seat height so your knee has a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Sit upright with a relaxed grip on the handlebars. Pedal at a comfortable cadence and adjust resistance as needed. Maintain steady breathing throughout. Vary intensity with interval or steady-state sessions.

description: Running is a fundamental cardiovascular exercise that improves aerobic capacity, burns calories, and strengthens the legs. It can be performed outdoors or on a treadmill at varying intensities.
tips: Start with a brisk walking warm-up. Gradually increase to a comfortable jogging pace. Maintain an upright posture with a slight forward lean. Land mid-foot beneath your center of mass. Keep arms relaxed and bent at 90 degrees. Breathe rhythmically. Gradually increase distance and pace over time.

description: The crunch is the most basic core isolation exercise targeting the rectus abdominis. It uses a shortened range of motion compared to a sit-up to reduce hip flexor involvement.
tips: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Place your hands behind your head or crossed over your chest. Curl your shoulders off the floor by contracting your abs, keeping your lower back in contact with the floor. Squeeze at the top. Lower back down with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The bicycle crunch is a rotational ab exercise that targets both the rectus abdominis and the obliques simultaneously by combining a crunch with alternating knee drives and torso rotation.
tips: Lie on your back with hands behind your head and knees bent at 90 degrees in the air. Lift your shoulders off the floor. Bring your right knee toward your chest while rotating your left shoulder toward it. Simultaneously extend your left leg. Switch sides in a continuous pedaling motion. Breathe steadily and avoid pulling on your neck.

description: The cable crunch uses a high cable with a rope attachment to add resistance to spinal flexion, making it the most progressive crunch variation for building rectus abdominis thickness.
tips: Attach a rope to a high cable pulley. Kneel in front of the machine and grip the rope behind your head with palms facing each other. Crunch downward by flexing your spine, bringing your elbows toward your knees. Squeeze your abs at the bottom. Return with control to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: Battle ropes are a high-intensity functional training tool that develops cardiovascular fitness, upper body endurance, and grip strength through alternating or simultaneous wave patterns.
tips: Anchor the rope to a fixed point and hold one end in each hand. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and knees slightly bent. Generate waves by alternating arm movements up and down with maximum power. Keep your core braced and maintain good posture throughout. Perform for desired time intervals.

description: The barbell curl is the gold-standard bicep mass exercise. Standing with a barbell held at arm's length, you curl the bar up to shoulder height while keeping the elbows stationary. It primarily targets the biceps brachii.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and hold the barbell with an underhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Keep elbows close to your sides. Curl the barbell up toward your chest, exhaling as you lift. Pause at the top and squeeze your biceps. Lower back to starting position, inhaling as you lower. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The dumbbell curl is a foundational bicep exercise that allows independent arm movement, helping to correct strength imbalances between sides. It targets the biceps brachii and brachialis.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand with arms fully extended and palms facing forward. Keep elbows close to your sides. Curl the dumbbells up toward your shoulders. Squeeze at the top. Lower back to starting position with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The concentration curl is a strict bicep isolation exercise performed seated with the upper arm braced against the inner thigh. It eliminates body english and targets the bicep peak with high precision.
tips: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor and knees slightly apart. Hold a dumbbell in one hand and place your elbow on the inside of your thigh just above the knee with arm fully extended, palm facing up. Curl the weight up toward your shoulder, keeping your elbow stationary. Pause and squeeze at the top. Slowly lower back down. Complete reps then switch arms.

description: The cable curl is a bicep isolation exercise that provides constant tension on the muscle throughout the full range of motion, unlike free weights which lose tension at the top.
tips: Attach a straight bar or rope to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the machine with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the handle with an underhand grip. Keep elbows close to your sides and curl the handles up toward your shoulders. Hold for a second at the top, then slowly lower back down. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The leg curl is an isolation exercise for the hamstrings performed on a machine in lying, seated, or standing position. It is essential for balanced leg development and knee health.
tips: Set up on the leg curl machine following its design (lying, seated, or standing). Adjust the pad to the back of your lower legs just above the ankles. Curl your legs toward your glutes by flexing your hamstrings. Squeeze at the top. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The lying leg curl is the most common hamstring isolation exercise, performed face-down on a machine. The prone position maximally stretches the hamstrings at the start for a greater range of motion.
tips: Lie face down on the leg curl machine and position the roller pad just above your Achilles tendon. Grip the handles for stability. Curl your legs toward your glutes by flexing your hamstrings. Squeeze at the top of the movement. Lower with control back to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The seated leg curl targets the hamstrings from a seated position where the hip is flexed, placing the hamstrings under greater stretch for a different stimulus than the lying version.
tips: Sit on the seated leg curl machine and adjust the pads so they rest just above the ankles. Grip the handles. Curl your legs down and back by flexing your hamstrings. Squeeze at the bottom of the movement. Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The incline dumbbell curl is performed on an incline bench, which pre-stretches the bicep at the bottom for a greater range of motion and increased long head activation.
tips: Set an adjustable bench to a 45-60 degree incline. Sit back with a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down. Curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders simultaneously. Squeeze the biceps at the top. Lower slowly back to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The hammer curl uses a neutral (palms-facing) grip to target the brachialis and brachioradialis in addition to the biceps, helping build overall arm thickness and forearm development.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing each other (neutral grip). Keep elbows close to your sides. Curl the dumbbells up toward your shoulders without rotating your wrists. Pause at the top. Lower slowly back to starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The Nordic curl is the gold standard for eccentric hamstring strengthening and injury prevention. It targets the long head of the biceps femoris through its full eccentric range — the portion of hamstring function most associated with strains and tears. Consistently included in athletic performance and physical therapy programs but absent from most fitness app libraries.
tips: Kneel on a padded surface with your feet anchored under a stable object or held by a partner. Keep your body in a straight line from knees to head. With hands ready to catch yourself, slowly lower your torso toward the floor by allowing the knees to extend — fight gravity with your hamstrings the entire way down. When you can no longer control the descent, use your hands to catch yourself and push back to the start. Perform 3x4-6 reps.
commonMistakes: This exercise is extremely challenging. Start with the assisted version: use hands to push back up from the floor. Full Nordic curls require significant hamstring strength. Lower as slowly as possible — the eccentric phase is the entire point of the exercise. Anchor feet under a sturdy object or have a partner hold your ankles.

description: The preacher curl uses a preacher bench pad to brace the upper arm, eliminating body sway and forcing the biceps to do all the work. It provides excellent isolation with emphasis on the lower portion of the bicep.
tips: Sit at a preacher bench and place the back of your upper arms flat on the pad. Grip the barbell or dumbbells with an underhand grip. Start with arms nearly fully extended. Curl the weight up toward your shoulders. Squeeze the biceps at the top. Lower slowly and with control back to near full extension. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The dead bug is an anti-extension core exercise that strengthens the deep abs and protects the lower back by maintaining a neutral spine while moving opposite limbs.
tips: Lie on your back with arms extended toward the ceiling and knees bent at 90 degrees in the air (tabletop). Press your lower back firmly into the floor. Lower your right arm overhead and extend your left leg simultaneously toward the floor without touching. Return to starting position. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating for desired reps.

description: The pull-up is one of the most demanding bodyweight upper body exercises. It targets the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and biceps using an overhand grip and full range of motion.
tips: Grip an overhead bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand (pronated) grip. Hang with arms fully extended. Pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar by driving your elbows down and back. Lower with control to a full hang. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The assisted pull-up machine uses a counterbalanced weight to reduce effective body weight, allowing users to build lat and bicep strength before performing unassisted pull-ups.
tips: Set the assistance weight on the machine. Kneel or stand on the platform and grip the overhead handles slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Pull yourself up until your chin clears the bar by driving your elbows down and back. Lower with control to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The Australian pull-up (also called inverted row) is a horizontal pulling exercise performed with a low bar or table. It targets the lats, rhomboids, and biceps and is an excellent bodyweight row progression.
tips: Set a bar or table at hip height. Lie underneath it and grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Straighten your body with only heels touching the floor. Pull your chest up to the bar by squeezing your shoulder blades together. Lower with control to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The chin-up is a bodyweight vertical pulling exercise using a supinated (underhand) grip that emphasizes the biceps alongside the lats, making it a bicep and back compound movement.
tips: Grip an overhead bar with hands shoulder-width apart using an underhand (supinated) grip. Hang with arms fully extended. Pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar by driving your elbows toward your hips. Lower with control back to a full hang. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The hanging leg raise is a more demanding version of the knee raise, extending the legs straight for greater lever arm and lower ab activation. Requires significant core strength.
tips: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip. Keeping legs straight and together, raise them until they are parallel to the floor or higher. Squeeze the abs at the top. Lower with control. Avoid swinging. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The floor leg raise targets the lower abs and hip flexors by raising straight legs from the floor. The long lever arm makes it more demanding than knee raises.
tips: Lie flat on your back with hands under your glutes for support or at your sides. Keep legs straight and together. Raise your legs until they are perpendicular to the floor or as high as possible. Slowly lower them back toward the floor without touching. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The hanging knee raise targets the lower abs and hip flexors by raising the knees toward the chest while hanging from a bar. It also develops grip strength.
tips: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Let your body hang fully. Raise your knees toward your chest by contracting your abs. Hold briefly at the top. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The calf raise is an isolation exercise for the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles of the lower leg. It can be performed standing or seated with bodyweight or added load.
tips: Stand with feet hip-width apart and the balls of your feet on the edge of a step or flat on the floor. Rise up onto your tiptoes by contracting your calves. Hold briefly at the top. Lower your heels as far down as possible. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The standing calf raise targets the gastrocnemius, the larger calf muscle that is visible from the outside. Performed standing with legs straight to maximize gastrocnemius activation.
tips: Stand on the edge of a step or calf raise machine with feet hip-width apart. Keep legs straight. Lower your heels below the step for a full stretch. Press up onto your tiptoes. Squeeze at the top. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The seated calf raise specifically targets the soleus muscle (the deeper calf) because the knee is bent, which de-emphasizes the gastrocnemius. Essential for complete calf development.
tips: Sit on the seated calf raise machine with your thighs under the pads and the balls of your feet on the step. Lower your heels as far as possible to get a full stretch. Press up onto your tiptoes by contracting your calves. Hold at the top. Lower slowly. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The trap 3 raise (also called lower trap raise) is a floor-based exercise targeting the lower trapezius — one of the most underactivated muscles in the upper body. Lower trap weakness leads to winging scapulae, impingement risk, and poor shoulder stability in overhead movements.
tips: Lie face down on an inclined surface or flat floor. Extend one arm at a 135° angle from your torso (Y position). Thumb pointing up. Raise the arm by depressing and retracting the shoulder blade — not by lifting with the arm. Hold 2-3 seconds at top. Lower slowly. Perform 3x10 per side.
commonMistakes: Keep the elbow straight. The thumb points up. Movement should come purely from the shoulder blade depressing and retracting — not from swinging the arm. Start without weight.

description: The front raise isolates the anterior (front) deltoid by raising weight directly in front of the body. It complements lateral raises and pressing for complete shoulder development.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding dumbbells or a plate in front of your thighs. Keeping elbows nearly straight, raise the weight directly in front of you to shoulder height. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The lateral raise isolates the medial (side) deltoid by abducting the arm against gravity with a dumbbell. It is the primary exercise for developing shoulder width.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding dumbbells at your sides. With a slight bend at the elbows, raise both arms out to the sides until they reach shoulder height. Pause briefly. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The cable lateral raise uses a low cable to provide constant tension throughout the lateral deltoid abduction, unlike dumbbells which lose tension at the bottom. It is highly effective for side delt isolation.
tips: Attach a single handle to a low cable pulley. Stand sideways to the machine and grip the handle with the far hand. With a slight bend in the elbow, raise your arm out to the side until it reaches shoulder height. Lower with control. Complete reps then switch sides.

description: The elliptical provides a low-impact full-body cardiovascular workout by combining leg and arm movements in a smooth oval motion. It reduces joint stress compared to running.
tips: Step onto the elliptical and grip the moving handles. Begin pedaling in a smooth elliptical motion with feet flat on the pads. Push and pull the handles to engage the upper body. Maintain an upright posture. Adjust resistance and incline to increase intensity. Perform for desired duration.

description: Movimiento de protracción y retracción escapular en posición de plancha. Enseña a controlar las escápulas, base de todo empuje y tracción sanos.
tips: En posición de plancha alta con los codos extendidos y bloqueados. Deja caer el pecho juntando las escápulas y después empuja el suelo separándolas al máximo. Todo el recorrido sale de la espalda alta: los codos no se doblan.
commonMistakes: Flexionar los codos y convertirlo en una flexión; mover la cadera arriba y abajo; recorrido demasiado corto; perder la línea del cuerpo.

description: The sled push is a functional strength and conditioning exercise that develops lower body power, cardiovascular endurance, and full-body strength through horizontal force production.
tips: Load the sled with appropriate weight. Place both hands on the poles at shoulder height. Lean forward at about 45 degrees and drive the sled forward by pushing through your legs with powerful strides. Keep your back flat and core braced throughout. Push for desired distance.

description: The barbell shrug allows heavier loading than dumbbell shrugs, making it the primary choice for upper trapezius hypertrophy. It is particularly important for users performing heavy overhead pressing and pull-up variations.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a barbell with an overhand grip in front of your thighs. Keep arms straight. Shrug shoulders straight up toward your ears. Hold at the top for 1 second. Lower back to the starting position under control. Perform 4 sets of 10-12 reps.
commonMistakes: Use straps if grip fails before traps. No rolling motion — pure vertical shrug. Keep the bar close to your legs. A slight forward lean is acceptable with heavy weight.

description: The dumbbell shrug is the most direct upper trapezius exercise. Despite its simplicity, it is one of the most commonly omitted exercises in beginner programs, leading to trapezius weakness and the characteristic rounded-shoulder posture.
tips: Stand holding dumbbells at your sides with a neutral grip. Keep arms straight. Elevate your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as possible. Hold for 1-2 seconds at the top. Lower slowly back to start. Perform 3-4 sets of 12-15 reps.
commonMistakes: Do not roll the shoulders — straight up and down only. Hold at the top for 1-2 seconds. Use a weight that allows full elevation without forward lean.

description: The stair climber simulates stair climbing to develop cardiovascular fitness and strengthen the glutes, quads, and calves. It provides a lower-impact alternative to running.
tips: Step onto the machine and grip the handrails lightly for balance only. Begin stepping at a comfortable pace. Push through each step with your full foot for maximum glute engagement. Keep an upright posture and avoid leaning heavily on the rails. Adjust speed as fitness improves. Perform for desired duration.

description: Mountain climbers are a dynamic core exercise that combines plank stability with alternating knee drives. They challenge the abs, hip flexors, and provide a cardiovascular stimulus.
tips: Start in a high plank position with hands under shoulders and body in a straight line. Drive one knee toward your chest while keeping the other leg extended. Quickly switch legs in a running motion. Continue alternating as fast as possible while maintaining a neutral spine. Perform for desired reps or time.

description: The standing quadriceps stretch targets the rectus femoris and hip flexors by bending the knee and pulling the foot toward the glutes while standing. Essential for leg day recovery.
tips: Stand on one leg and bend the other knee, bringing your foot behind you toward your glutes. Hold your ankle with the same-side hand. Keep your knees together and stand tall. Hold 20-30 seconds. Switch legs. Use a wall for balance if needed.

description: The hip flexor stretch targets the iliopsoas and rectus femoris by placing the hip in extension. It counteracts the tightness caused by prolonged sitting and improves posture.
tips: Kneel on one knee with the other foot forward in a lunge position. Keeping your back straight, shift your hips forward gently until you feel a stretch at the front of the back leg's hip. Squeeze the back glute to intensify the stretch. Hold 20-30 seconds. Switch sides.

description: The wrist flexor stretch targets the forearm flexors that are stressed during pulling and gripping exercises. It helps prevent tendinitis and carpal tunnel symptoms.
tips: Extend one arm in front of you with palm facing up. Use your other hand to gently bend your wrist down so your fingers point toward the floor. Apply gentle pressure to deepen the stretch. Hold 20-30 seconds. Switch hands.

description: The shoulder cross-body stretch targets the posterior deltoid and rotator cuff by pulling the arm across the body. It is essential after pressing and pulling exercises for shoulder recovery.
tips: Stand tall and bring one arm straight across your chest at shoulder height. Use your other arm to gently press it closer to your chest. Feel the stretch in the back of the shoulder and upper arm. Hold 20-30 seconds. Switch arms.

description: The standing toe touch stretch targets the hamstrings and lower back through a forward bend. It improves posterior chain flexibility and is a common warm-up or cool-down movement.
tips: Stand with feet hip-width apart and legs straight. Hinge at the hips and reach your hands toward the floor or your toes. Allow your upper body to hang and breathe into the stretch. For a deeper stretch, round your back slightly and relax your neck. Hold for 20-30 seconds. Slowly roll back up to standing.

description: The cat-cow stretch is a flowing spinal mobility exercise that alternates between spinal flexion (cat) and extension (cow). It mobilizes the entire spine and is ideal as a warm-up or cool-down.
tips: Start in tabletop position on hands and knees. Inhale into Cow: drop your belly toward the floor, lift your chest and chin, let your tailbone rise. Exhale into Cat: round your spine upward, tuck your chin to your chest, tuck your tailbone under. Alternate slowly for 8-12 cycles, syncing breath with movement.

description: The neck side stretch gently lengthens the sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius muscles on one side of the neck. It relieves tension from overhead pressing and poor posture.
tips: Sit or stand tall. Tilt your right ear toward your right shoulder while keeping your left shoulder pressed down. For a deeper stretch, place your right hand gently on your head for slight overpressure. Hold 20-30 seconds. Switch sides.

description: The open book stretch is a supine thoracic mobility exercise that combines thoracic rotation with chest opening. It is one of the most effective exercises for reversing rounded shoulder posture and improving thoracic extension simultaneously, making it ideal as part of any warm-up or cool-down.
tips: Lie on your side with knees stacked and bent at 90°. Extend both arms in front of you at shoulder height. Keeping the knees together and lower hand on the floor, slowly rotate the top arm open across your body toward the floor on the other side, following it with your eyes and head. Hold 2-3 seconds. Return to start. Perform 8-10 reps per side.
commonMistakes: Let gravity do most of the work on the rotating arm. Keep the knees stacked together throughout — do not let them separate. Breathe deeply into the stretch and try to add a bit more range with each exhale.

description: The leg extension is a quad isolation exercise performed on a machine. It targets the rectus femoris and other quadriceps muscles through knee extension without hip flexion.
tips: Sit on the leg extension machine and adjust the roller pad to just above your ankles. Grip the handles. Extend your legs by contracting your quadriceps until legs are nearly straight. Squeeze the quads at the top. Lower with control to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The cable triceps pushdown is one of the most common tricep exercises, performed at a cable machine. It effectively isolates all three heads of the triceps through constant tension.
tips: Attach a straight bar or rope to a high cable pulley. Stand facing the machine with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the bar with an overhand grip at about chest height. Keep your elbows pinned to your sides. Push the bar down until your arms are fully extended. Squeeze the triceps. Slowly return to starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

nameEs: Extensión de tríceps por encima de la cabeza
description: The overhead triceps extension stretches the triceps long head fully by placing the arm overhead, providing a unique stimulus compared to pushdown variations. Can be performed with dumbbells, cable, or barbell.
tips: Hold a dumbbell with both hands and raise it overhead with arms fully extended. Keep your elbows pointing forward and close to your head. Lower the dumbbell behind your head by bending at the elbows until your forearms are parallel to the floor. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The face pull is a cable exercise targeting the rear delts, rotator cuff, and upper traps. It is an essential exercise for shoulder health, posture correction, and balanced upper body development.
tips: Attach a rope to a high cable pulley. Stand facing the machine and grip each end of the rope with palms facing each other. Pull the rope toward your face with elbows flared high. Squeeze your rear delts and upper traps at the end. Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The wide push-up places hands wider than shoulder-width to increase chest activation compared to standard push-ups. It targets the pectoralis major with reduced tricep involvement.
tips: Start in a plank position with hands placed wider than shoulder-width apart. Keep your body in a straight line from head to heels. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows out to the sides. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The archer push-up extends one arm wide while pressing with the other for unilateral chest and tricep loading. It is a key progression between standard push-ups and one-arm push-ups.
tips: Start in a wide push-up position with hands much wider than shoulders. Shift your weight to one side and bend that elbow to lower your chest toward that hand, while keeping the other arm nearly straight out to the side. Press back up through the bent arm. Repeat on the same side for all reps then switch. Aim for 6 to 10 reps per side.

description: The push-up is a foundational bodyweight compound exercise targeting the pectoralis major, triceps, and anterior deltoids. It requires no equipment and can be progressively loaded through variations.
tips: Start in a high plank with hands shoulder-width apart, body in a straight line from head to heels. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows at about 45 degrees. Stop just before your chest touches the ground. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The serratus push-up (also called scapular push-up) specifically targets the serratus anterior — the muscle responsible for scapular protraction and upward rotation. It is the foundation for all calisthenics skills requiring shoulder stability: handstands, planche progressions, and dips. Often missing from beginner programs despite being essential for shoulder health.
tips: Start in the top push-up position with arms fully extended. Without bending the elbows, push the floor away by rounding your upper back and allowing the shoulder blades to spread wide (protract). Hold 2 seconds at the top. Lower by letting the shoulder blades come together (retract). Keep the core engaged throughout. Perform 3x12-15.
commonMistakes: The range of motion is very small — only 2-3 cm of scapular movement. Focus on the sensation of pushing the floor away at the very top of a regular push-up position. Do not bend the elbows. This is a scapular exercise, not an arm exercise.

description: The decline push-up is performed with feet elevated, increasing the angle and shifting emphasis to the upper chest and anterior deltoids. The higher the feet, the more shoulder-dominant the movement becomes.
tips: Place your feet on an elevated surface (bench, chair, or step) and hands on the floor shoulder-width apart. Keep your body in a straight line. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The diamond push-up places hands close together forming a diamond shape, shifting emphasis from the chest to the triceps. It is one of the most effective bodyweight triceps exercises.
tips: Start in a plank position with hands placed close together directly under your chest, forming a diamond shape with your index fingers and thumbs. Lower your chest toward your hands. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The pike push-up is a bodyweight shoulder pressing exercise performed in an inverted V position. You set your hips high with hands and feet on the floor, and lower your head toward the floor by bending at the elbows. It is the primary bodyweight progression toward handstand push-ups.
tips: Start in a push-up position. Walk your feet toward your hands, raising your hips high into an inverted V. Your body should form a sharp angle at the hips with head between your arms. Bend at the elbows to lower the top of your head toward the floor. Lower until your head nearly touches. Press back up to the pike position by extending your arms. Keep your hips high throughout. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set.
commonMistakes: stretching

description: The handstand push-up is an advanced bodyweight overhead pressing movement that develops the deltoids and triceps against full bodyweight. It requires significant shoulder strength and balance.
tips: Kick up into a handstand against a wall with hands shoulder-width apart. Lower your head toward the floor by bending your elbows. Stop just before your head touches. Press back up to the starting position. Maintain a tight core and straight body throughout. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The incline push-up is an easier push-up variation with hands elevated on a surface. It reduces bodyweight load, making it suitable for beginners or as a warm-up movement.
tips: Place your hands on an elevated surface such as a bench, step, or wall at shoulder-width. Keep your body in a straight line from head to heels. Lower your chest toward the surface. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The pseudo planche push-up positions the hands by the hips and leans the body forward, placing extreme load on the anterior deltoids and chest. It is a key skill in the planche progression.
tips: Get into a push-up position and rotate your hands so fingers point toward your feet, placing them beside your lower ribcage or hips. Lean your bodyweight forward so your shoulders are ahead of your hands. Lower your chest toward the floor. Press back up. Maintain a straight body throughout. Aim for 5 to 10 reps.

description: Dips are a fundamental bodyweight compound movement targeting the triceps, chest, and anterior deltoids. Performed on parallel bars, they allow full depth loading of the triceps.
tips: Grip parallel bars and push up to the starting position with arms fully extended. Cross your feet behind you if desired. Lean slightly forward and lower your body by bending at the elbows. Continue until your upper arms are parallel to the floor. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: Assisted dips use a machine or band to offset body weight, allowing beginners to build tricep and chest strength before progressing to unassisted dips.
tips: Set the assistance weight on the machine. Kneel or stand on the pad as directed by the machine design. Grip the parallel bars with arms fully extended. Lower your body by bending at the elbows until your upper arms are parallel to the floor. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The bench dip is a bodyweight triceps exercise performed using a bench or chair. It targets the triceps with assistance from the anterior deltoid and chest.
tips: Sit on the edge of a bench or chair and place your hands next to your hips with fingers facing forward. Slide your hips off the bench and extend your legs in front of you. Bend your elbows to lower your body toward the floor until your arms are at about 90 degrees. Push back up to the starting position by straightening your arms. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The bear crawl is a full-body movement where you crawl on all fours with knees hovering just above the floor. It develops core stability, shoulder strength, and cardiovascular conditioning simultaneously.
tips: Start on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Lift your knees one inch off the floor. Move forward by simultaneously moving your right hand and left foot, then your left hand and right foot. Keep your hips low and core engaged. Avoid letting your hips rise or rotate. Crawl for desired distance or time.

description: The Russian twist is a rotational core exercise targeting the obliques and rectus abdominis. It can be performed with bodyweight or added load from a medicine ball, dumbbell, or plate.
tips: Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet slightly off the ground. Lean back slightly while keeping your back straight. Hold your hands together or grip a weight in front of you. Rotate your torso to one side, then the other in a controlled motion. Repeat for desired reps per side.

description: The medicine ball slam is a power exercise that develops explosive full-body strength and cardiovascular conditioning. It targets the lats, abs, and shoulders through a maximal overhead to floor throwing motion.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding a medicine ball. Raise the ball overhead with arms extended. Engage your core and slam the ball into the floor as hard as possible by contracting your abs and lats. Catch the ball on the bounce or pick it up. Repeat immediately for desired reps.

description: The hip thrust is the most effective exercise for gluteus maximus development. Performed with the upper back on a bench and a barbell across the hips, it provides peak glute contraction under load.
tips: Place your upper back against a bench with a barbell across your hips. Plant your feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Drive through your heels to thrust your hips up until your body is parallel to the floor. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Lower your hips to the floor. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The single-leg hip thrust is a unilateral glute exercise that provides intense isolation of one glute at a time, helping to identify and correct strength imbalances between sides.
tips: Place your upper back against a bench with one foot flat on the floor and the other leg raised with knee bent at 90 degrees or extended. Drive through the planted heel to thrust your hips up until your body is parallel to the floor. Squeeze the working glute hard at the top. Lower your hips toward the floor. Complete all reps then switch legs.

description: The hyperextension (back extension) exercise targets the lower back erectors, glutes, and hamstrings. Performed on a hyperextension bench, it strengthens the posterior chain for injury prevention.
tips: Position yourself face down on a hyperextension bench with your hips at the pad edge. Cross your arms over your chest or hold a weight plate. Lower your upper body toward the floor by hinging at the hips. Raise back up until your body forms a straight line. Avoid hyperextending beyond neutral at the top. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The hollow body hold is a gymnastics-based isometric core exercise that trains the abs, hip flexors, and serratus anterior simultaneously. It develops deep core stability crucial for advanced bodyweight skills.
tips: Lie on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight. Press your lower back into the floor by engaging your core. Lift your shoulders and legs off the floor simultaneously, keeping your legs together and arms close to your ears. Hold the hollow banana shape with lower back pressed to the floor. Breathe steadily and hold for desired duration.

description: Sprint intervals alternate between maximum effort sprints and rest periods to develop speed, anaerobic capacity, and cardiovascular fitness while burning significant calories.
tips: Warm up with 5-10 minutes of jogging. Sprint at maximum effort for 20-40 seconds. Rest or walk for 60-90 seconds. Repeat for 6-10 rounds. Cool down with 5 minutes of light jogging and stretching. Adjust sprint and rest durations to your fitness level.

description: The lat pulldown is a cable machine exercise that mimics the pull-up motion. It targets the latissimus dorsi with adjustable resistance, making it accessible for all fitness levels.
tips: Sit at the lat pulldown machine and secure your thighs under the pad. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Pull the bar down to your upper chest by driving your elbows toward your hips. Squeeze your lats at the bottom. Slowly raise the bar back to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The wide-grip lat pulldown uses a wider-than-shoulder hand position to increase the stretch on the lat at the top and emphasize the outer lats for a wider back appearance.
tips: Sit at the lat pulldown machine and grip the bar wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Secure thighs under the pad. Pull the bar down to your upper chest by driving your elbows toward the floor. Squeeze your lats at the bottom. Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The straight-arm pulldown isolates the lats by keeping the elbows straight, removing bicep involvement. It provides a strong lat contraction at the bottom of each rep.
tips: Attach a rope or straight bar to a high cable pulley. Stand facing the machine and grip the attachment with arms extended overhead. Keep a slight bend in the elbows. Pull the bar down and back toward your thighs in a sweeping arc. Squeeze the lats at the bottom. Return to starting position with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The L-sit is an advanced gymnastics-based hold performed on parallel bars, rings, or the floor. It simultaneously trains the abs, hip flexors, triceps, and shoulders under isometric tension.
tips: Grip parallel bars or dip handles and push yourself up with arms straight. Raise both legs in front of you to hip height, forming an L-shape with your body. Keep your legs straight and feet flexed. Hold for desired duration while keeping arms straight and shoulders depressed. Lower with control.

description: The ab crunch machine provides a guided resistance for core flexion, targeting the rectus abdominis with adjustable weight and reduced hip flexor involvement.
tips: Adjust the machine seat and select the desired weight. Sit with your back flat and grip the handles or pads. Crunch forward by flexing your spine, bringing your ribcage toward your hips. Squeeze your abs at the bottom. Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The lateral band walk trains the glute medius dynamically, making it more sport-specific and functionally relevant than static exercises. It activates the glute medius through the full gait cycle and is particularly valuable as a warm-up before squats, lunges, or any lower body session.
tips: Place a resistance band just above your knees. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart in a slight squat position. Step sideways with your right foot, then follow with your left, maintaining tension in the band throughout. Keep the core tight and torso upright. Take 10-15 steps in each direction for 3 sets.
commonMistakes: Keep a slight squat position throughout — do not stand fully upright between steps. Steps should be controlled, not bouncy. Keep feet parallel, toes forward. The band goes just above the knees.

description: The inchworm is a dynamic mobility and warm-up exercise that stretches the hamstrings while simultaneously engaging the shoulders and core. It prepares the body for training.
tips: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hinge at the hips and place your hands on the floor. Walk your hands forward until you reach a plank position. Perform a push-up (optional). Walk your feet toward your hands by taking small steps until you feel a hamstring stretch. Return to standing. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The rear delt fly targets the posterior deltoid and upper back muscles by performing a horizontal abduction with dumbbells while bent forward. It is essential for shoulder balance and posture.
tips: Hinge forward at the hips until torso is nearly parallel to the floor. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with arms hanging straight down, palms facing each other. Raise both arms out to the sides by squeezing the rear delts and upper back. Pause at the top. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The cable kickback isolates the gluteus maximus using a low cable pulley with an ankle attachment. The constant cable tension throughout the range of motion makes it superior to bodyweight kickbacks.
tips: Attach an ankle cuff to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the machine and hold the frame for balance. Shift weight to one leg. Kick the working leg back and up by contracting the glute, keeping the leg nearly straight. Squeeze at the top. Lower with control. Complete reps then switch legs.

description: The cable triceps kickback isolates the triceps using a low cable pulley. The cable provides constant tension throughout the movement unlike dumbbell kickbacks.
tips: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position with a single handle attachment. Stand facing the machine and hinge forward at the hips. Hold the handle with one hand and brace your upper arm against your torso, elbow bent at 90 degrees. Extend your arm back fully, squeezing the tricep at the top. Return to starting position with control. Complete reps then switch arms.

description: The reverse pec deck uses a machine to perform horizontal abduction targeting the rear delts and rhomboids. The chest-supported position and guided path provide excellent isolation.
tips: Sit facing the pec deck machine. Grip the handles with arms extended forward. Pull the handles back and outward in a wide arc by squeezing your rear delts and shoulder blades together. Pause at the end range. Return with control to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: Aperturas de pecho en máquina guiada. Aísla el pectoral con la trayectoria fija de la máquina, sin exigir estabilización, por lo que permite buscar el fallo con seguridad.
tips: Ajusta el asiento de forma que las empuñaduras queden a la altura del pecho. Apoya la espalda completa en el respaldo. Junta los brazos describiendo un arco y aprieta el pectoral 1 segundo en el punto de máxima contracción. Vuelve controlado sin dejar que el peso choque.
commonMistakes: Subir el asiento de más y convertirlo en un ejercicio de hombro; separar la espalda del respaldo para empujar con el cuerpo; bloquear los codos; soltar el peso de golpe en la vuelta.

description: The deadlift is the king of posterior chain exercises, training the entire back, glutes, hamstrings, and traps simultaneously. It is one of the most effective movements for total body strength.
tips: Stand with feet hip-width apart and the bar over your mid-foot. Hinge at the hips and grip the bar just outside your legs. Take a deep breath, brace your core, and engage your lats. Drive through the floor to lift the bar, keeping it close to your body. Lock out hips and knees at the top. Lower with control to the floor. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The stiff-leg deadlift is a hamstring hinge exercise performed with straight legs to maximize the stretch on the hamstrings. It differs from the RDL by keeping legs completely straight.
tips: Stand holding a barbell or dumbbells with legs completely straight or with a very minimal knee bend. Hinge at the hips and lower the weight toward the floor while keeping your back flat. Feel the deep hamstring and lower back stretch at the bottom. Return to standing by extending your hips. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The Romanian deadlift (RDL) is a hip hinge movement with legs nearly straight that maximally stretches and loads the hamstrings under tension. It is the primary hamstring mass builder.
tips: Stand holding a barbell or dumbbells at hip level with feet hip-width apart. Push your hips back while lowering the weight down your legs, keeping a slight knee bend. Keep your back flat and maintain a neutral spine. Feel the hamstring stretch at the bottom. Drive your hips forward to return to standing. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The sumo deadlift uses a wide stance with a narrow grip, reducing the range of motion and shifting emphasis to the inner thighs, glutes, and quads compared to the conventional deadlift.
tips: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width and toes pointed out. Place hands inside your legs on the bar with an overhand or mixed grip. Push your knees out and keep your chest up. Drive through your legs to lift the bar, keeping it close to your body. Lock out hips and knees at the top. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The handstand hold is an isometric gymnastic skill that develops shoulder stability, upper body strength, and body awareness. It requires significant shoulder strength and balance practice.
tips: Place hands shoulder-width apart on the floor near a wall. Kick up into a handstand and find balance with heels against the wall. Engage your core, squeeze your glutes, and point your toes. Keep arms fully locked and shoulders pressed up. Breathe steadily. Hold for desired duration.

description: The plank is a fundamental isometric core exercise that develops anti-extension strength and endurance throughout the entire trunk. It requires no equipment and serves as the basis for many core progressions.
tips: Get into a push-up position and lower onto your forearms. Elbows directly under your shoulders. Keep your body in a perfectly straight line from head to heels. Engage your core, glutes, and quads. Breathe steadily. Avoid letting your hips sag or rise. Hold for the desired duration.

description: The plank shoulder tap adds a unilateral stability challenge to the standard plank by alternately touching opposite shoulders, forcing the core to resist rotation.
tips: Start in a high plank position with hands under shoulders and body in a straight line. Keep your feet hip-width apart for a wider base. Lift one hand and tap the opposite shoulder while preventing your hips from rotating. Place the hand back down and repeat on the other side. Move slowly and with control. Repeat for desired reps per side.

description: The side plank is an isometric lateral core exercise that specifically targets the obliques and quadratus lumborum. It builds lateral stability crucial for spine health and athletic performance.
tips: Lie on your side and prop yourself up on your forearm with your elbow under your shoulder. Stack your feet on top of each other. Raise your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight diagonal line. Keep your core engaged and hips square. Breathe steadily. Hold for desired duration then switch sides.

description: The pigeon pose is a deep hip stretch that targets the piriformis, glutes, and hip external rotators. It is especially beneficial after leg workouts and for those with tight hips from sitting.
tips: From a push-up position, bring one knee forward and place it behind your wrist with the foot toward the opposite hip. Extend the back leg behind you. Lower your hips toward the floor. Walk your hands forward and lower your chest toward the floor for a deeper stretch. Hold 30-60 seconds. Switch sides.

description: Child's pose is a restful yoga position that gently stretches the lats, lower back, glutes, and hip flexors. It is used as a recovery position and cool-down stretch.
tips: Kneel on the floor and sit your hips back onto your heels. Extend your arms forward on the floor and lower your forehead to the mat. Walk your hands forward to deepen the lat stretch. Breathe deeply into your lower back. Hold 30-60 seconds.

description: The leg press is a compound leg exercise using a machine to press weight away from the body. It targets the quads, glutes, and hamstrings with reduced spinal loading compared to the squat.
tips: Sit in the leg press machine with your back and head flat against the pad. Place feet hip-width apart on the platform. Release the safety handles. Lower the platform by bending your knees toward your chest. Press through your feet to extend your legs. Do not lock out knees at the top. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The Arnold press adds a rotation to the standard shoulder press, starting with palms facing you and rotating outward during the press. This recruits all three deltoid heads through the full range.
tips: Sit or stand holding dumbbells at shoulder height with palms facing you and elbows bent. Press the dumbbells up while simultaneously rotating your palms outward until they face away from you at the top. Lower in the reverse motion, rotating palms back toward you. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The landmine press is a one-arm pressing movement using a barbell anchored at one end. The angled pressing path is joint-friendly for shoulders while developing unilateral pressing strength.
tips: Anchor a barbell in a landmine attachment or corner. Stand perpendicular to the bar and hold the sleeve with one hand at shoulder height. Press the bar up and slightly forward at an angle. Extend fully at the top. Lower with control. Complete reps then switch sides.

description: The close-grip bench press is a barbell compound pressing exercise that shifts emphasis from the chest to the triceps by narrowing the grip. It also recruits the anterior deltoid.
tips: Lie on a flat bench and grip the barbell with hands shoulder-width apart or slightly closer. Unrack the bar and hold it above your chest with arms extended. Lower the bar to your lower chest while keeping elbows close to your torso. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The barbell bench press is the foundational horizontal pressing exercise for developing the pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps. It is one of the primary upper body mass builders.
tips: Lie on a flat bench and grip the barbell slightly wider than shoulder-width. Unrack the bar and hold it above your chest. Lower the bar to your mid-chest with elbows at about 45 degrees. Press back up to the starting position explosively. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The dumbbell bench press allows greater range of motion than the barbell version and requires more stabilizer muscle activation. It targets the pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps.
tips: Lie on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in each hand at chest level, elbows at about 45 degrees. Press the dumbbells up and together until arms are nearly extended. Lower back to chest level with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The dumbbell shoulder press is the primary overhead pressing exercise for deltoid development. It allows more natural wrist rotation and greater range of motion than the barbell version.
tips: Sit or stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height, palms facing forward. Press the dumbbells overhead until arms are nearly fully extended. Lower back to shoulder height. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The shoulder press machine provides a guided pressing motion for deltoid development with reduced stability demands, making it accessible for beginners or as an isolation finisher.
tips: Adjust the seat height so the handles are at shoulder level. Grip the handles and sit with your back flat against the pad. Press overhead until arms are nearly fully extended. Lower back to shoulder height. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The chest press machine provides a guided pressing motion that targets the pectoralis major, anterior deltoids, and triceps. The machine path makes it suitable for beginners.
tips: Adjust the seat so the handles are at chest height. Sit with your back flat against the pad. Grip the handles and press forward until arms are nearly fully extended. Squeeze your chest at the end. Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The machine chest press is a guided pressing exercise targeting the pectoralis major. The fixed path reduces the stabilization requirement, making it ideal for high-rep or isolation work.
tips: Adjust the seat height so handles align with your mid-chest. Sit with your back flat against the pad. Press the handles forward until your arms are nearly extended. Squeeze the chest at the end. Return with control to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The decline bench press targets the lower portion of the pectoralis major by pressing from a declined angle. It reduces anterior deltoid involvement compared to flat and incline pressing.
tips: Lie on a decline bench with feet secured and grip the barbell slightly wider than shoulder-width. Unrack the bar and hold it above your lower chest. Lower the bar to your lower chest. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The incline barbell bench press targets the upper portion of the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid by pressing from an angled position. It is essential for complete chest development.
tips: Set the bench to 30-45 degrees. Lie back and grip the barbell slightly wider than shoulder-width. Unrack and hold above your upper chest. Lower the bar to your upper chest with elbows at 45-60 degrees. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The incline dumbbell bench press targets the upper chest with greater range of motion than the barbell version. It allows each arm to work independently for balanced development.
tips: Set an adjustable bench to 30-45 degrees. Sit back holding a dumbbell in each hand at upper chest level. Press the dumbbells up and together until arms are nearly extended. Lower back with control to chest level. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The overhead press (OHP) is the fundamental barbell shoulder pressing exercise. It develops the deltoids, triceps, and upper traps while requiring significant core stability for the standing version.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and grip the barbell at shoulder height with hands just outside shoulder-width. Brace your core. Press the bar straight overhead until arms are fully extended. Lower back to shoulder height. Repeat for desired reps.

description: Ejercicio antirrotación para el core. No se trata de mover el peso, sino de resistir el giro que la polea intenta provocar. Trabaja la estabilidad profunda del tronco.
tips: Colócate de perfil a la polea con los pies a la anchura de los hombros. Sujeta el agarre con ambas manos a la altura del esternón. Extiende los brazos al frente y mantén 2-3 segundos resistiendo la rotación. Vuelve al pecho sin girar el tronco.
commonMistakes: Dejar que el tronco rote hacia la polea; usar demasiado peso y compensar con los brazos; contener la respiración; separar los pies del suelo o mover la cadera.

description: The seated dumbbell shoulder press provides upper body stability from the bench, allowing focus on deltoid development. Sitting removes the need for lower body bracing compared to the standing version.
tips: Sit on a bench with back support. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height, palms facing forward. Press the dumbbells overhead until arms are nearly fully extended. Lower back to shoulder height. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The glute bridge is a fundamental hip extension exercise that activates the gluteus maximus with minimal lower back stress. It is performed lying on the floor and is ideal for beginners or as a warm-up movement.
tips: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Drive through your heels to lift your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Lower your hips back to the floor. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The cable pull-through is a hip hinge movement using a low cable pulley that targets the glutes and hamstrings. It teaches proper hip hinge mechanics with constant cable tension.
tips: Attach a rope to a low cable pulley. Stand facing away from the machine and grip the rope between your legs. Hinge forward at the hips, letting the rope pull back between your thighs. Drive your hips forward explosively to stand upright, squeezing your glutes at the top. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The upright row pulls a barbell or dumbbells vertically up toward the chin, targeting the upper traps and medial deltoids simultaneously. It is a compound shoulder exercise.
tips: Stand holding a barbell with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Pull the bar straight up toward your chin, leading with your elbows. Elbows should reach above shoulder height. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: Rowing on an ergometer (rowing machine) is a full-body cardiovascular exercise that engages the legs, back, and arms in a coordinated pushing and pulling motion.
tips: Sit on the rowing machine and strap your feet in. Grip the handle with an overhand grip. Start with knees bent and arms extended (catch position). Drive through your legs first, then lean back slightly, then pull the handle to your lower ribcage. Return in reverse order: arms, lean forward, bend knees. Repeat continuously for desired duration.

description: The chest-supported row eliminates lower back involvement by lying face-down on an incline bench. It isolates the mid-back, rhomboids, and rear delts with strict form.
tips: Set an incline bench to 30-45 degrees. Lie face down with your chest on the pad and a dumbbell in each hand hanging straight down. Pull the dumbbells up toward your hips by driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades. Lower with control to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The barbell row is a fundamental compound back exercise that targets the lats, rhomboids, traps, and rear delts. It is one of the primary mass-building exercises for the back.
tips: Stand with feet hip-width apart and hinge forward until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Grip a barbell slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Pull the bar toward your lower chest or upper abdomen by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades at the top. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The single-arm dumbbell row is a unilateral back exercise that targets the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and rear delts. Supporting yourself on a bench allows heavy loading with good form.
tips: Place one knee and hand on a bench for support. Hold a dumbbell in the opposite hand with arm hanging straight down. Pull the dumbbell up toward your hip by driving your elbow back. Squeeze your lat at the top. Lower with control back to the starting position. Complete reps then switch sides.

description: Remo horizontal con barra guiada en máquina Smith. La guía elimina la necesidad de estabilizar la barra, lo que permite concentrarse en la espalda y cargar más que en el remo libre.
tips: Colócate con el tronco inclinado unos 45 grados y las rodillas ligeramente flexionadas. Agarre algo más ancho que los hombros. Lleva la barra hacia el abdomen bajo tirando con los codos, no con las manos. Aprieta las escápulas al final del recorrido.
commonMistakes: Incorporar el tronco a cada repetición para dar impulso; tirar hacia el pecho en vez de hacia el abdomen; redondear la zona lumbar; usar recorrido corto por exceso de peso.

description: The T-bar row is a compound rowing exercise using a landmine or T-bar apparatus. It allows heavy loading for the mid-back, lats, and rhomboids with a neutral or overhand grip.
tips: Position yourself over the T-bar with feet straddling the bar. Hinge forward at the hips until torso is roughly 45 degrees. Grip the handles and pull the bar toward your chest by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades at the top. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The scapular rear delt row uses a towel anchored in a door to replicate a horizontal row with a rear delt emphasis. It fills the gap left by Face Pull for home environments, training the posterior deltoid and rhomboids with no equipment other than a towel.
tips: Anchor a towel in a door at chest height. Hold each end, lean back with arms extended. Pull yourself in by driving elbows out wide to the sides (not back). Squeeze shoulder blades at the top. Slowly return. Adjust foot position to control difficulty. Perform 3x12-15.
commonMistakes: Elbows flare out — this is intentional and different from standard rows. The wide elbow position maximizes rear delt activation. Keep core tight.

description: The inverted row is a bodyweight horizontal pulling exercise performed under a bar, table, or using a towel. It trains the mid-back, rhomboids, and rear delts with scapular retraction.
tips: Position yourself under a bar set at hip height. Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Extend your body in a plank position with heels on the floor. Pull your chest up to the bar by driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades. Lower with control. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The seated row machine provides a guided horizontal pulling motion that targets the mid-back, rhomboids, and rear delts. The machine path ensures consistent form for beginners.
tips: Adjust the seat and chest pad height. Sit with your chest against the pad and grip the handles. Pull the handles toward your torso by squeezing your shoulder blades together. Hold briefly at full contraction. Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The seated cable row is a horizontal pulling exercise using a cable machine that targets the mid-back, lats, and rhomboids. The seated position and constant cable tension allow excellent muscle engagement.
tips: Sit at the cable row station with feet on the platform and knees slightly bent. Grip the handle with both hands and sit upright with arms extended. Pull the handle toward your lower abdomen by driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades. Hold briefly. Extend arms back to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: The single-arm cable row allows unilateral back training, helping to correct muscle imbalances between sides. It targets the lat, rhomboid, and rear delt with rotation and full range of motion.
tips: Set a cable pulley to mid height. Stand facing the machine and grip the single handle with one hand. Step back to create tension. Pull the handle toward your hip by driving your elbow back. Rotate your torso slightly at the end range. Squeeze your lat. Return to starting position with control. Complete reps then switch sides.

description: High knees are a running-in-place drill that elevates the heart rate and targets the hip flexors, quads, and core. The exaggerated knee lift develops running mechanics and cardiovascular fitness.
tips: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Drive one knee up toward your chest as high as possible while simultaneously hopping on the other foot. Pump your arms in opposition with your legs. Alternate legs at a fast pace. Keep your core engaged and maintain an upright posture. Perform for desired time or reps.

description: The skull crusher is a lying barbell or dumbbell tricep extension that heavily loads all three heads of the triceps with excellent range of motion. Performed on a flat bench.
tips: Lie on a flat bench holding a barbell or EZ bar with an overhand grip, arms extended directly above your chest. Keep your upper arms stationary and perpendicular to the floor. Bend at the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead or just above it. Press back up to the starting position. Repeat for desired reps.

description: Movilidad articular para el hombro. Calienta la articulación y prepara el manguito rotador antes de entrenar tren superior.
tips: De pie, brazos extendidos en cruz. Describe círculos progresivamente más amplios, primero hacia delante y después hacia atrás. Mantén el tronco firme y los hombros lejos de las orejas.
commonMistakes: Hacer círculos muy rápidos y pequeños en vez de amplios y controlados; encoger los hombros; arquear la zona lumbar para ganar amplitud.

description: Deslizamiento de brazos por la pared. Mejora la movilidad de hombro en flexión y la rotación externa, y corrige la postura de hombros adelantados.
tips: Espalda, glúteos y cabeza apoyados en la pared. Antebrazos contra la pared formando una W. Desliza los brazos hacia arriba hasta la Y sin despegar muñecas ni codos, y baja controlado.
commonMistakes: Despegar la zona lumbar de la pared arqueando la espalda; perder el contacto de las muñecas al subir; forzar el rango con dolor; encoger los hombros.

nameEs: Rotación interna y externa del fémur
description: Movilidad de cadera en rotación. Recupera el rango que se pierde al pasar muchas horas sentado y mejora la profundidad de la sentadilla.
tips: Sentado en el suelo con las rodillas flexionadas y los pies separados más que la cadera. Deja caer ambas rodillas a un lado y luego al otro, manteniendo los pies apoyados. Movimiento lento, sin rebotes.
commonMistakes: Hacerlo con impulso en vez de controlado; despegar los pies del suelo; forzar hasta el dolor; olvidar trabajar los dos lados por igual.

description: Thoracic rotation in quadruped is an active mobility drill that restores rotational range of motion in the thoracic spine — the segment most commonly stiff in desk workers and gym users. Limited thoracic rotation forces compensation at the lumbar spine and shoulders, causing back pain and impingement. This exercise directly addresses that pattern.
tips: Start on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Place one hand behind your head. Rotate your upper body, bringing that elbow toward the floor first (under the torso), then rotate upward to reach the elbow toward the ceiling. Follow the elbow with your eyes. Keep hips square and still. Perform 10 rotations per side for 2-3 sets.
commonMistakes: Keep the hips still — only the thoracic spine rotates. Place a hand behind the head and rotate the elbow toward the ceiling. The goal is to feel a stretch in the mid-back, not the lower back. Move slowly and breathe into the rotation.

description: The ab wheel rollout is an advanced anti-extension core exercise that challenges the entire core from a kneeling or standing position. It develops both strength and stability.
tips: Kneel on a mat and grip an ab wheel with both hands. Place the wheel on the floor in front of you. Slowly roll the wheel forward, extending your body as far as you can while keeping your core tight and lower back neutral. Roll back to the starting position by contracting your abs and pulling the wheel back under you. Repeat for desired reps.

description: Jump rope is a high-intensity cardio exercise that improves cardiovascular endurance, coordination, and calf strength. It can be performed with various techniques including basic, skipping, and double-under.
tips: Hold the rope handles at hip height, one in each hand. Swing the rope overhead and jump with both feet as it passes under you. Land softly on the balls of your feet. Keep a slight bend in the knees and maintain an upright posture. Vary pace and footwork patterns as fitness improves.

description: The box jump is a plyometric exercise that develops lower body explosive power and reactive strength. Landing on a box reduces joint impact compared to depth jumps.
tips: Stand facing a sturdy box with feet shoulder-width apart. Bend your knees into a quarter squat and swing your arms back. Explosively jump onto the box, swinging your arms forward for momentum. Land softly with both feet flat on the box and knees slightly bent. Stand up fully. Step back down (do not jump down). Repeat for desired reps.

description: The skater jump is a plyometric lateral movement that mimics a speed skater's stride. It develops lateral power, hip stability, and single-leg strength while elevating cardiovascular demand.
tips: Start in a slight squat on your right leg. Jump laterally to the left and land softly on your left foot, allowing your right leg to swing behind. Immediately push off the left foot and jump back to the right. Reach toward the landing foot with the opposite hand each time. Maintain a low athletic position throughout.

description: The jumping jack is a classic full-body cardio exercise that simultaneously abducts the arms and legs then returns them. It elevates heart rate quickly and improves cardiovascular endurance.
tips: Stand with feet together and arms at your sides. Jump and simultaneously spread your feet wider than shoulder-width while raising your arms above your head. Jump again to return to the starting position with feet together and arms at your sides. Repeat at a brisk pace for desired reps or time.

description: The bodyweight squat is the foundational lower-body movement: a hip- and knee-dominant pattern that builds quad, glute, and core strength with no equipment. It is the base of the legs progression toward lunges, split squats, and the pistol squat.
tips: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. Brace your core and push your hips back as you bend your knees, lowering until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor. Keep your chest up and knees tracking over your toes. Drive through your heels to return to standing. Perform 3 sets of 15-25 reps.
